case_info.scenario: A man in his 60s presented to the clinic with a several-day history of nontender, nonitchy purpuric rash on his scalp. The patient denied using any over-the-counter or prescription topicals at the affected sites before the onset of the eruption except for petroleum jelly. His medical history was significant for chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and allergic contact dermatitis. The patient reported being started on ibrutinib and allopurinol therapy 6 weeks prior to the rash onset for treatment of CLL. Physical examination revealed multiple purpuric, nonblanchable macules and patches on the frontal, vertex, temporal, and parietal scalp (Figure, A). A punch biopsy specimen from the scalp was obtained for histopathologic analysis (Figure, B).
case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of petechial eruption on the scalp. B, Punch biopsy specimen (hematoxylin-eosin).
case_info.explanation: Ibrutinib is a selective Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for treatment of several lymphoproliferative disorders, including CLL, mantle cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, and Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Skin eruptions represent a frequent adverse effect of the medication and are seen in up to 47% of patients who take it.1 A retrospective cohort study by Iberri et al2reported 2 main types of skin eruptions associated with ibrutinib use: an asymptomatic, nonpalpable, petechial rash, and a palpable, purpuric eruption resembling leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV). The nonpalpable eruption had late rash onset (80 days after initiation of the drug on average) and mild associated symptoms. The palpable eruption was associated with earlier rash onset (15 days after initiation of the drug on average) and worse severity, requiring temporary interruption of ibrutinib therapy in some of the patients. All the patients who required temporary interruption of therapy were able to resume ibrutinib.2Histopathology of the eruptions revealed perivascular and interstitial inflammation and erythrocyte extravasation with no evidence of LCV. Interestingly, ibrutinib has been associated with bleeding complications in patients undergoing cutaneous surgery.3Increased bleeding is postulated to be due to the inhibition caused by ibrutinib of 2 platelet-expressed family kinases, BTK and TEC, which are involved in platelet glycoprotein VI signaling.4Inhibition of platelet aggregation may contribute to the development of petechial eruptions and ecchymoses commonly associated with ibrutinib therapy. Additionally, a recently published study5reported an overlap of cutaneous toxicities from ibrutinib with those of selective epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors. A total of 10 out of 19 patients in the study developed acneiform papulopustular reactions, resembling those of EGFR inhibitors.5Ibrutinib has been shown to inhibit EGFR in a dose-dependent manner, which likely accounts for overlap in cutaneous toxicities between the drugs. Inhibition of EGFR is known to cause apoptosis of basal keratinocytes, as well as disruption of cellular proliferation, differentiation, and migration. These effects can lead to loss of stratum corneum integrity, sebaceous gland dysfunction, and reduction in major components of cornified cell envelope. In addition, inflammatory cytokines, released by epithelial cells, trigger leukocyte recruitment and tissue damage with subsequent keratinocyte apoptosis, vascular dilation, increased permeability, and red blood cell extravasation.6Interestingly, EGFR inhibitors have also been known to induce purpuric drug eruptions, which are thought to be the result of endothelial inflammation leading to increased vascular permeability and red blood cell extravasation.7Thus, EGFR inhibition may also play a part in the pathogenesis of petechial eruptions seen with ibrutinib. Differential diagnoses of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption include LCV, immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis affecting postcapillary venules in the dermis. Palpable purpura is the most common clinical manifestation of LCV, but purpuric macules may be seen initially.8This condition differs from ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption histologically, presenting with small-vessel vasculitis and prominent leukocytoclasis. Conversely, ITP is an autoimmune bleeding disorder characterized by decreased platelet counts, which presents with petechiae, ecchymoses, and nonpalpable purpura.9Histologically, ITP demonstrates extravasated erythrocytes in the dermis without associated perivascular inflammation, unlike ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption. Finally, TTP represents a subtype of the thrombotic microangiopathy syndromes caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. This condition is characterized by a pentad of findings consisting of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological abnormalities, fever, and renal dysfunction.10Purpuric rash is the most common skin manifestation of the disease, with platelet and fibrin thrombi and erythrocyte extravasation seen on histology. We present a case of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption, which represents one of the most common skin toxicities of the drug. Ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption tends to be mild in severity and usually does not require dose adjustment or medication discontinuation. Oncologists should be familiar with ibrutinib-associated toxic effects associated with skin as its use continues to gain more widespread application in treatment of various neoplastic conditions.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

The patient reported being started on ibrutinib and allopurinol therapy 6 weeks prior to the rash onset for treatment of CLL. case_info.explanation: Ibrutinib is a selective Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for treatment of several lymphoproliferative disorders, including CLL, mantle cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, and Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Skin eruptions represent a frequent adverse effect of the medication and are seen in up to 47% of patients who take it.1 A retrospective cohort study by Iberri et al2reported 2 main types of skin eruptions associated with ibrutinib use: an asymptomatic, nonpalpable, petechial rash, and a palpable, purpuric eruption resembling leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV). The nonpalpable eruption had late rash onset (80 days after initiation of the drug on average) and mild associated symptoms. The palpable eruption was associated with earlier rash onset (15 days after initiation of the drug on average) and worse severity, requiring temporary interruption of ibrutinib therapy in some of the patients. All the patients who required temporary interruption of therapy were able to resume ibrutinib.2Histopathology of the eruptions revealed perivascular and interstitial inflammation and erythrocyte extravasation with no evidence of LCV. Interestingly, ibrutinib has been associated with bleeding complications in patients undergoing cutaneous surgery.3Increased bleeding is postulated to be due to the inhibition caused by ibrutinib of 2 platelet-expressed family kinases, BTK and TEC, which are involved in platelet glycoprotein VI signaling.4Inhibition of platelet aggregation may contribute to the development of petechial eruptions and ecchymoses commonly associated with ibrutinib therapy. Additionally, a recently published study5reported an overlap of cutaneous toxicities from ibrutinib with those of selective epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors. A total of 10 out of 19 patients in the study developed acneiform papulopustular reactions, resembling those of EGFR inhibitors.5Ibrutinib has been shown to inhibit EGFR in a dose-dependent manner, which likely accounts for overlap in cutaneous toxicities between the drugs. Inhibition of EGFR is known to cause apoptosis of basal keratinocytes, as well as disruption of cellular proliferation, differentiation, and migration. These effects can lead to loss of stratum corneum integrity, sebaceous gland dysfunction, and reduction in major components of cornified cell envelope. In addition, inflammatory cytokines, released by epithelial cells, trigger leukocyte recruitment and tissue damage with subsequent keratinocyte apoptosis, vascular dilation, increased permeability, and red blood cell extravasation.6Interestingly, EGFR inhibitors have also been known to induce purpuric drug eruptions, which are thought to be the result of endothelial inflammation leading to increased vascular permeability and red blood cell extravasation.7Thus, EGFR inhibition may also play a part in the pathogenesis of petechial eruptions seen with ibrutinib. Differential diagnoses of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption include LCV, immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis affecting postcapillary venules in the dermis. Palpable purpura is the most common clinical manifestation of LCV, but purpuric macules may be seen initially.8This condition differs from ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption histologically, presenting with small-vessel vasculitis and prominent leukocytoclasis. Conversely, ITP is an autoimmune bleeding disorder characterized by decreased platelet counts, which presents with petechiae, ecchymoses, and nonpalpable purpura.9Histologically, ITP demonstrates extravasated erythrocytes in the dermis without associated perivascular inflammation, unlike ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption. Finally, TTP represents a subtype of the thrombotic microangiopathy syndromes caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. This condition is characterized by a pentad of findings consisting of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological abnormalities, fever, and renal dysfunction.10Purpuric rash is the most common skin manifestation of the disease, with platelet and fibrin thrombi and erythrocyte extravasation seen on histology. We present a case of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption, which represents one of the most common skin toxicities of the drug. Ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption tends to be mild in severity and usually does not require dose adjustment or medication discontinuation. Oncologists should be familiar with ibrutinib-associated toxic effects associated with skin as its use continues to gain more widespread application in treatment of various neoplastic conditions.

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

The patient denied using any over-the-counter or prescription topicals at the affected sites before the onset of the eruption except for petroleum jelly. His medical history was significant for chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and allergic contact dermatitis. The patient reported being started on ibrutinib and allopurinol therapy 6 weeks prior to the rash onset for treatment of CLL. Physical examination revealed multiple purpuric, nonblanchable macules and patches on the frontal, vertex, temporal, and parietal scalp (Figure, A). A punch biopsy specimen from the scalp was obtained for histopathologic analysis (Figure, B).
case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of petechial eruption on the scalp. B, Punch biopsy specimen (hematoxylin-eosin).
case_info.explanation: Ibrutinib is a selective Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for treatment of several lymphoproliferative disorders, including CLL, mantle cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, and Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Skin eruptions represent a frequent adverse effect of the medication and are seen in up to 47% of patients who take it.1 A retrospective cohort study by Iberri et al2reported 2 main types of skin eruptions associated with ibrutinib use: an asymptomatic, nonpalpable, petechial rash, and a palpable, purpuric eruption resembling leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV). The nonpalpable eruption had late rash onset (80 days after initiation of the drug on average) and mild associated symptoms. The palpable eruption was associated with earlier rash onset (15 days after initiation of the drug on average) and worse severity, requiring temporary interruption of ibrutinib therapy in some of the patients. All the patients who required temporary interruption of therapy were able to resume ibrutinib.2Histopathology of the eruptions revealed perivascular and interstitial inflammation and erythrocyte extravasation with no evidence of LCV. Interestingly, ibrutinib has been associated with bleeding complications in patients undergoing cutaneous surgery.3Increased bleeding is postulated to be due to the inhibition caused by ibrutinib of 2 platelet-expressed family kinases, BTK and TEC, which are involved in platelet glycoprotein VI signaling.4Inhibition of platelet aggregation may contribute to the development of petechial eruptions and ecchymoses commonly associated with ibrutinib therapy. Additionally, a recently published study5reported an overlap of cutaneous toxicities from ibrutinib with those of selective epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors. A total of 10 out of 19 patients in the study developed acneiform papulopustular reactions, resembling those of EGFR inhibitors.5Ibrutinib has been shown to inhibit EGFR in a dose-dependent manner, which likely accounts for overlap in cutaneous toxicities between the drugs. Inhibition of EGFR is known to cause apoptosis of basal keratinocytes, as well as disruption of cellular proliferation, differentiation, and migration. These effects can lead to loss of stratum corneum integrity, sebaceous gland dysfunction, and reduction in major components of cornified cell envelope. In addition, inflammatory cytokines, released by epithelial cells, trigger leukocyte recruitment and tissue damage with subsequent keratinocyte apoptosis, vascular dilation, increased permeability, and red blood cell extravasation.6Interestingly, EGFR inhibitors have also been known to induce purpuric drug eruptions, which are thought to be the result of endothelial inflammation leading to increased vascular permeability and red blood cell extravasation.7Thus, EGFR inhibition may also play a part in the pathogenesis of petechial eruptions seen with ibrutinib. Differential diagnoses of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption include LCV, immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis affecting postcapillary venules in the dermis. Palpable purpura is the most common clinical manifestation of LCV, but purpuric macules may be seen initially.8This condition differs from ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption histologically, presenting with small-vessel vasculitis and prominent leukocytoclasis. Conversely, ITP is an autoimmune bleeding disorder characterized by decreased platelet counts, which presents with petechiae, ecchymoses, and nonpalpable purpura.9Histologically, ITP demonstrates extravasated erythrocytes in the dermis without associated perivascular inflammation, unlike ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption. Finally, TTP represents a subtype of the thrombotic microangiopathy syndromes caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. This condition is characterized by a pentad of findings consisting of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological abnormalities, fever, and renal dysfunction.10Purpuric rash is the most common skin manifestation of the disease, with platelet and fibrin thrombi and erythrocyte extravasation seen on histology. We present a case of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption, which represents one of the most common skin toxicities of the drug. Ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption tends to be mild in severity and usually does not require dose adjustment or medication discontinuation. Oncologists should be familiar with ibrutinib-associated toxic effects associated with skin as its use continues to gain more widespread application in treatment of various neoplastic conditions.

case_info.explanation: Ibrutinib is a selective Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for treatment of several lymphoproliferative disorders, including CLL, mantle cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, and Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Skin eruptions represent a frequent adverse effect of the medication and are seen in up to 47% of patients who take it.1 A retrospective cohort study by Iberri et al2reported 2 main types of skin eruptions associated with ibrutinib use: an asymptomatic, nonpalpable, petechial rash, and a palpable, purpuric eruption resembling leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV). The nonpalpable eruption had late rash onset (80 days after initiation of the drug on average) and mild associated symptoms. The palpable eruption was associated with earlier rash onset (15 days after initiation of the drug on average) and worse severity, requiring temporary interruption of ibrutinib therapy in some of the patients. All the patients who required temporary interruption of therapy were able to resume ibrutinib.2Histopathology of the eruptions revealed perivascular and interstitial inflammation and erythrocyte extravasation with no evidence of LCV. Interestingly, ibrutinib has been associated with bleeding complications in patients undergoing cutaneous surgery.3Increased bleeding is postulated to be due to the inhibition caused by ibrutinib of 2 platelet-expressed family kinases, BTK and TEC, which are involved in platelet glycoprotein VI signaling.4Inhibition of platelet aggregation may contribute to the development of petechial eruptions and ecchymoses commonly associated with ibrutinib therapy. Additionally, a recently published study5reported an overlap of cutaneous toxicities from ibrutinib with those of selective epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors. A total of 10 out of 19 patients in the study developed acneiform papulopustular reactions, resembling those of EGFR inhibitors.5Ibrutinib has been shown to inhibit EGFR in a dose-dependent manner, which likely accounts for overlap in cutaneous toxicities between the drugs. Inhibition of EGFR is known to cause apoptosis of basal keratinocytes, as well as disruption of cellular proliferation, differentiation, and migration. These effects can lead to loss of stratum corneum integrity, sebaceous gland dysfunction, and reduction in major components of cornified cell envelope. In addition, inflammatory cytokines, released by epithelial cells, trigger leukocyte recruitment and tissue damage with subsequent keratinocyte apoptosis, vascular dilation, increased permeability, and red blood cell extravasation.6Interestingly, EGFR inhibitors have also been known to induce purpuric drug eruptions, which are thought to be the result of endothelial inflammation leading to increased vascular permeability and red blood cell extravasation.7Thus, EGFR inhibition may also play a part in the pathogenesis of petechial eruptions seen with ibrutinib. Differential diagnoses of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption include LCV, immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis affecting postcapillary venules in the dermis. Palpable purpura is the most common clinical manifestation of LCV, but purpuric macules may be seen initially.8This condition differs from ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption histologically, presenting with small-vessel vasculitis and prominent leukocytoclasis. Conversely, ITP is an autoimmune bleeding disorder characterized by decreased platelet counts, which presents with petechiae, ecchymoses, and nonpalpable purpura.9Histologically, ITP demonstrates extravasated erythrocytes in the dermis without associated perivascular inflammation, unlike ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption. Finally, TTP represents a subtype of the thrombotic microangiopathy syndromes caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. This condition is characterized by a pentad of findings consisting of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological abnormalities, fever, and renal dysfunction.10Purpuric rash is the most common skin manifestation of the disease, with platelet and fibrin thrombi and erythrocyte extravasation seen on histology. We present a case of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption, which represents one of the most common skin toxicities of the drug. Ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption tends to be mild in severity and usually does not require dose adjustment or medication discontinuation. Oncologists should be familiar with ibrutinib-associated toxic effects associated with skin as its use continues to gain more widespread application in treatment of various neoplastic conditions.

case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of petechial eruption on the scalp. B, Punch biopsy specimen (hematoxylin-eosin).
case_info.explanation: Ibrutinib is a selective Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for treatment of several lymphoproliferative disorders, including CLL, mantle cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, and Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Skin eruptions represent a frequent adverse effect of the medication and are seen in up to 47% of patients who take it.1 A retrospective cohort study by Iberri et al2reported 2 main types of skin eruptions associated with ibrutinib use: an asymptomatic, nonpalpable, petechial rash, and a palpable, purpuric eruption resembling leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV). The nonpalpable eruption had late rash onset (80 days after initiation of the drug on average) and mild associated symptoms. The palpable eruption was associated with earlier rash onset (15 days after initiation of the drug on average) and worse severity, requiring temporary interruption of ibrutinib therapy in some of the patients. All the patients who required temporary interruption of therapy were able to resume ibrutinib.2Histopathology of the eruptions revealed perivascular and interstitial inflammation and erythrocyte extravasation with no evidence of LCV. Interestingly, ibrutinib has been associated with bleeding complications in patients undergoing cutaneous surgery.3Increased bleeding is postulated to be due to the inhibition caused by ibrutinib of 2 platelet-expressed family kinases, BTK and TEC, which are involved in platelet glycoprotein VI signaling.4Inhibition of platelet aggregation may contribute to the development of petechial eruptions and ecchymoses commonly associated with ibrutinib therapy. Additionally, a recently published study5reported an overlap of cutaneous toxicities from ibrutinib with those of selective epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors. A total of 10 out of 19 patients in the study developed acneiform papulopustular reactions, resembling those of EGFR inhibitors.5Ibrutinib has been shown to inhibit EGFR in a dose-dependent manner, which likely accounts for overlap in cutaneous toxicities between the drugs. Inhibition of EGFR is known to cause apoptosis of basal keratinocytes, as well as disruption of cellular proliferation, differentiation, and migration. These effects can lead to loss of stratum corneum integrity, sebaceous gland dysfunction, and reduction in major components of cornified cell envelope. In addition, inflammatory cytokines, released by epithelial cells, trigger leukocyte recruitment and tissue damage with subsequent keratinocyte apoptosis, vascular dilation, increased permeability, and red blood cell extravasation.6Interestingly, EGFR inhibitors have also been known to induce purpuric drug eruptions, which are thought to be the result of endothelial inflammation leading to increased vascular permeability and red blood cell extravasation.7Thus, EGFR inhibition may also play a part in the pathogenesis of petechial eruptions seen with ibrutinib. Differential diagnoses of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption include LCV, immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis affecting postcapillary venules in the dermis. Palpable purpura is the most common clinical manifestation of LCV, but purpuric macules may be seen initially.8This condition differs from ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption histologically, presenting with small-vessel vasculitis and prominent leukocytoclasis. Conversely, ITP is an autoimmune bleeding disorder characterized by decreased platelet counts, which presents with petechiae, ecchymoses, and nonpalpable purpura.9Histologically, ITP demonstrates extravasated erythrocytes in the dermis without associated perivascular inflammation, unlike ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption. Finally, TTP represents a subtype of the thrombotic microangiopathy syndromes caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. This condition is characterized by a pentad of findings consisting of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological abnormalities, fever, and renal dysfunction.10Purpuric rash is the most common skin manifestation of the disease, with platelet and fibrin thrombi and erythrocyte extravasation seen on histology. We present a case of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption, which represents one of the most common skin toxicities of the drug. Ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption tends to be mild in severity and usually does not require dose adjustment or medication discontinuation. Oncologists should be familiar with ibrutinib-associated toxic effects associated with skin as its use continues to gain more widespread application in treatment of various neoplastic conditions.

1. Mental Demand

   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied

   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.

   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal

       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

case_info.explanation: Ibrutinib is a selective Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for treatment of several lymphoproliferative disorders, including CLL, mantle cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, and Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Skin eruptions represent a frequent adverse effect of the medication and are seen in up to 47% of patients who take it.1 A retrospective cohort study by Iberri et al2reported 2 main types of skin eruptions associated with ibrutinib use: an asymptomatic, nonpalpable, petechial rash, and a palpable, purpuric eruption resembling leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV). The nonpalpable eruption had late rash onset (80 days after initiation of the drug on average) and mild associated symptoms. The palpable eruption was associated with earlier rash onset (15 days after initiation of the drug on average) and worse severity, requiring temporary interruption of ibrutinib therapy in some of the patients. All the patients who required temporary interruption of therapy were able to resume ibrutinib.2Histopathology of the eruptions revealed perivascular and interstitial inflammation and erythrocyte extravasation with no evidence of LCV. Interestingly, ibrutinib has been associated with bleeding complications in patients undergoing cutaneous surgery.3Increased bleeding is postulated to be due to the inhibition caused by ibrutinib of 2 platelet-expressed family kinases, BTK and TEC, which are involved in platelet glycoprotein VI signaling.4Inhibition of platelet aggregation may contribute to the development of petechial eruptions and ecchymoses commonly associated with ibrutinib therapy. Additionally, a recently published study5reported an overlap of cutaneous toxicities from ibrutinib with those of selective epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors. A total of 10 out of 19 patients in the study developed acneiform papulopustular reactions, resembling those of EGFR inhibitors.5Ibrutinib has been shown to inhibit EGFR in a dose-dependent manner, which likely accounts for overlap in cutaneous toxicities between the drugs. Inhibition of EGFR is known to cause apoptosis of basal keratinocytes, as well as disruption of cellular proliferation, differentiation, and migration. These effects can lead to loss of stratum corneum integrity, sebaceous gland dysfunction, and reduction in major components of cornified cell envelope. In addition, inflammatory cytokines, released by epithelial cells, trigger leukocyte recruitment and tissue damage with subsequent keratinocyte apoptosis, vascular dilation, increased permeability, and red blood cell extravasation.6Interestingly, EGFR inhibitors have also been known to induce purpuric drug eruptions, which are thought to be the result of endothelial inflammation leading to increased vascular permeability and red blood cell extravasation.7Thus, EGFR inhibition may also play a part in the pathogenesis of petechial eruptions seen with ibrutinib. Differential diagnoses of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption include LCV, immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis affecting postcapillary venules in the dermis. Palpable purpura is the most common clinical manifestation of LCV, but purpuric macules may be seen initially.8This condition differs from ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption histologically, presenting with small-vessel vasculitis and prominent leukocytoclasis. Conversely, ITP is an autoimmune bleeding disorder characterized by decreased platelet counts, which presents with petechiae, ecchymoses, and nonpalpable purpura.9Histologically, ITP demonstrates extravasated erythrocytes in the dermis without associated perivascular inflammation, unlike ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption. Finally, TTP represents a subtype of the thrombotic microangiopathy syndromes caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. This condition is characterized by a pentad of findings consisting of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological abnormalities, fever, and renal dysfunction.10Purpuric rash is the most common skin manifestation of the disease, with platelet and fibrin thrombi and erythrocyte extravasation seen on histology. We present a case of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption, which represents one of the most common skin toxicities of the drug. Ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption tends to be mild in severity and usually does not require dose adjustment or medication discontinuation. Oncologists should be familiar with ibrutinib-associated toxic effects associated with skin as its use continues to gain more widespread application in treatment of various neoplastic conditions.

case_info.scenario: A man in his 60s presented to the clinic with a several-day history of nontender, nonitchy purpuric rash on his scalp. The patient denied using any over-the-counter or prescription topicals at the affected sites before the onset of the eruption except for petroleum jelly. His medical history was significant for chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and allergic contact dermatitis. The patient reported being started on ibrutinib and allopurinol therapy 6 weeks prior to the rash onset for treatment of CLL. Physical examination revealed multiple purpuric, nonblanchable macules and patches on the frontal, vertex, temporal, and parietal scalp (Figure, A). case_info.explanation: Ibrutinib is a selective Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for treatment of several lymphoproliferative disorders, including CLL, mantle cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, and Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Skin eruptions represent a frequent adverse effect of the medication and are seen in up to 47% of patients who take it.1 A retrospective cohort study by Iberri et al2reported 2 main types of skin eruptions associated with ibrutinib use: an asymptomatic, nonpalpable, petechial rash, and a palpable, purpuric eruption resembling leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV). The nonpalpable eruption had late rash onset (80 days after initiation of the drug on average) and mild associated symptoms. The palpable eruption was associated with earlier rash onset (15 days after initiation of the drug on average) and worse severity, requiring temporary interruption of ibrutinib therapy in some of the patients. All the patients who required temporary interruption of therapy were able to resume ibrutinib.2Histopathology of the eruptions revealed perivascular and interstitial inflammation and erythrocyte extravasation with no evidence of LCV. Interestingly, ibrutinib has been associated with bleeding complications in patients undergoing cutaneous surgery.3Increased bleeding is postulated to be due to the inhibition caused by ibrutinib of 2 platelet-expressed family kinases, BTK and TEC, which are involved in platelet glycoprotein VI signaling.4Inhibition of platelet aggregation may contribute to the development of petechial eruptions and ecchymoses commonly associated with ibrutinib therapy. Additionally, a recently published study5reported an overlap of cutaneous toxicities from ibrutinib with those of selective epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors. A total of 10 out of 19 patients in the study developed acneiform papulopustular reactions, resembling those of EGFR inhibitors.5Ibrutinib has been shown to inhibit EGFR in a dose-dependent manner, which likely accounts for overlap in cutaneous toxicities between the drugs. Inhibition of EGFR is known to cause apoptosis of basal keratinocytes, as well as disruption of cellular proliferation, differentiation, and migration. These effects can lead to loss of stratum corneum integrity, sebaceous gland dysfunction, and reduction in major components of cornified cell envelope. In addition, inflammatory cytokines, released by epithelial cells, trigger leukocyte recruitment and tissue damage with subsequent keratinocyte apoptosis, vascular dilation, increased permeability, and red blood cell extravasation.6Interestingly, EGFR inhibitors have also been known to induce purpuric drug eruptions, which are thought to be the result of endothelial inflammation leading to increased vascular permeability and red blood cell extravasation.7Thus, EGFR inhibition may also play a part in the pathogenesis of petechial eruptions seen with ibrutinib. Differential diagnoses of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption include LCV, immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis affecting postcapillary venules in the dermis. Palpable purpura is the most common clinical manifestation of LCV, but purpuric macules may be seen initially.8This condition differs from ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption histologically, presenting with small-vessel vasculitis and prominent leukocytoclasis. Conversely, ITP is an autoimmune bleeding disorder characterized by decreased platelet counts, which presents with petechiae, ecchymoses, and nonpalpable purpura.9Histologically, ITP demonstrates extravasated erythrocytes in the dermis without associated perivascular inflammation, unlike ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption. Finally, TTP represents a subtype of the thrombotic microangiopathy syndromes caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. This condition is characterized by a pentad of findings consisting of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological abnormalities, fever, and renal dysfunction.10Purpuric rash is the most common skin manifestation of the disease, with platelet and fibrin thrombi and erythrocyte extravasation seen on histology. We present a case of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption, which represents one of the most common skin toxicities of the drug. Ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption tends to be mild in severity and usually does not require dose adjustment or medication discontinuation. Oncologists should be familiar with ibrutinib-associated toxic effects associated with skin as its use continues to gain more widespread application in treatment of various neoplastic conditions.

case_info.scenario: A man in his 60s presented to the clinic with a several-day history of nontender, nonitchy purpuric rash on his scalp. The patient denied using any over-the-counter or prescription topicals at the affected sites before the onset of the eruption except for petroleum jelly. His medical history was significant for chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and allergic contact dermatitis. The patient reported being started on ibrutinib and allopurinol therapy 6 weeks prior to the rash onset for treatment of CLL. Physical examination revealed multiple purpuric, nonblanchable macules and patches on the frontal, vertex, temporal, and parietal scalp (Figure, A). A punch biopsy specimen from the scalp was obtained for histopathologic analysis (Figure, B).
case_info.caption: A, Clinical image of petechial eruption on the scalp. B, Punch biopsy specimen (hematoxylin-eosin).
case_info.explanation: Ibrutinib is a selective Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor used for treatment of several lymphoproliferative disorders, including CLL, mantle cell lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma, and Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Skin eruptions represent a frequent adverse effect of the medication and are seen in up to 47% of patients who take it.1 A retrospective cohort study by Iberri et al2reported 2 main types of skin eruptions associated with ibrutinib use: an asymptomatic, nonpalpable, petechial rash, and a palpable, purpuric eruption resembling leukocytoclastic vasculitis (LCV). The nonpalpable eruption had late rash onset (80 days after initiation of the drug on average) and mild associated symptoms. The palpable eruption was associated with earlier rash onset (15 days after initiation of the drug on average) and worse severity, requiring temporary interruption of ibrutinib therapy in some of the patients. All the patients who required temporary interruption of therapy were able to resume ibrutinib.2Histopathology of the eruptions revealed perivascular and interstitial inflammation and erythrocyte extravasation with no evidence of LCV. Interestingly, ibrutinib has been associated with bleeding complications in patients undergoing cutaneous surgery.3Increased bleeding is postulated to be due to the inhibition caused by ibrutinib of 2 platelet-expressed family kinases, BTK and TEC, which are involved in platelet glycoprotein VI signaling.4Inhibition of platelet aggregation may contribute to the development of petechial eruptions and ecchymoses commonly associated with ibrutinib therapy. Additionally, a recently published study5reported an overlap of cutaneous toxicities from ibrutinib with those of selective epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitors. A total of 10 out of 19 patients in the study developed acneiform papulopustular reactions, resembling those of EGFR inhibitors.5Ibrutinib has been shown to inhibit EGFR in a dose-dependent manner, which likely accounts for overlap in cutaneous toxicities between the drugs. Inhibition of EGFR is known to cause apoptosis of basal keratinocytes, as well as disruption of cellular proliferation, differentiation, and migration. These effects can lead to loss of stratum corneum integrity, sebaceous gland dysfunction, and reduction in major components of cornified cell envelope. In addition, inflammatory cytokines, released by epithelial cells, trigger leukocyte recruitment and tissue damage with subsequent keratinocyte apoptosis, vascular dilation, increased permeability, and red blood cell extravasation.6Interestingly, EGFR inhibitors have also been known to induce purpuric drug eruptions, which are thought to be the result of endothelial inflammation leading to increased vascular permeability and red blood cell extravasation.7Thus, EGFR inhibition may also play a part in the pathogenesis of petechial eruptions seen with ibrutinib. Differential diagnoses of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption include LCV, immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP), and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is a small-vessel vasculitis affecting postcapillary venules in the dermis. Palpable purpura is the most common clinical manifestation of LCV, but purpuric macules may be seen initially.8This condition differs from ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption histologically, presenting with small-vessel vasculitis and prominent leukocytoclasis. Conversely, ITP is an autoimmune bleeding disorder characterized by decreased platelet counts, which presents with petechiae, ecchymoses, and nonpalpable purpura.9Histologically, ITP demonstrates extravasated erythrocytes in the dermis without associated perivascular inflammation, unlike ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption. Finally, TTP represents a subtype of the thrombotic microangiopathy syndromes caused by severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. This condition is characterized by a pentad of findings consisting of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological abnormalities, fever, and renal dysfunction.10Purpuric rash is the most common skin manifestation of the disease, with platelet and fibrin thrombi and erythrocyte extravasation seen on histology. We present a case of ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption, which represents one of the most common skin toxicities of the drug. Ibrutinib-induced petechial eruption tends to be mild in severity and usually does not require dose adjustment or medication discontinuation. Oncologists should be familiar with ibrutinib-associated toxic effects associated with skin as its use continues to gain more widespread application in treatment of various neoplastic conditions.
